Executive Summary
1.	Accidental Release Prevention and Emergency Response Policies
At the Future Foam plant in Mansfield, MA we handle toluene diisocyanate (TDI), which is considered hazardous and regulated by the EPA. The same properties that make TDI valuable for use at our facility also make it necessary to observe certain safety precautions in the handling of the substance. Safety precautions have been implemented to prevent unnecessary human exposure, to reduce the threat to our own personal health as well as to our co-workers, and to reduce the threat to nearby members of our community. It is our policy to adhere to all applicable federal and state rules and regulations.
Future Foam is committed to the safety of our employees and the public, and to the preservation of the environment, through the prevention of accidental releases of hazardous substances. Successful implementation of our accidental release prevention program will help ensure that emergencies are unlikely and reduce the likelihood that emergency response procedures will be needed. Nevertheless, an emergency, such as a release of TDI, is possible. Emergency response procedures are in place to help ensure that accidents will be mitigated properly without undue risk to the public, environment, employees, contractors, or other personnel within the plant.

2.	Regulated Process and Substance
The primary purpose of this facility is to produce flexible polyurethane foam, which is sold to other facilities and used to produce bedding, furniture and a number of other products. TDI is one of the reactants required to produce polyurethane foam. TDI is received by rail car and by tank truck, and is stored in indoor storage tanks. TDI is stored in seven (7) 9,900 gal process tanks, and a maximum of one (1) 190,000 lb railcars. The total capacity of all tanks and rail cars is about 900,000 pounds of TDI. The TDI is piped to a mix head where it is mixed with other reactants to produce a slab of polyurethane foam

. The foam is conveyed to cutting stations where it is cut to the size and shape specified by our customers.
TDI is the only substance handled at our plant that is regulated by EPAs risk management program (RMP) rule. TDI is covered because the maximum quantity stored onsite exceed EPAs threshold quantity (TQ) of 10,000 pounds.

3.	Accidental Release Prevention and Specific Prevention Steps
This facility has implemented programs and procedures that comply with EPAs Program Level 1 requirements. The facility qualifies for Level 1 coverage because (1) the modeling using approved methods shows that no public receptors are located within the distance to the toxic endpoint in the event of a worst-case scenario release of TDI, and (2) TDI is not a substance covered by OSHAs process safety management standard (PSM). Our accidental release program is designed to systematically accomplish the following functions:
	Conduct hazard reviews to identify, evaluate, and control process hazards associated with the regulated substances, processes, and procedures Five-Year Accident History
	Create, maintain, and evaluate operating procedures for activities within or near processes that use regulated substances
	Provide training for personnel who operate covered processes so that they safely perform their jobs
	Monitor and control maintenance activities that can affect the mechanical integrity of equipment used in covered processes
	Periodically review the RMP and related practices to ensure that the facility's procedures and programs are adequate to address all of the requirements of the RMP rule
	Ensure that process incidents, particularly those of catastrophic magnitude or potential, are thoroughly investigated using our incident investigation procedures and that relevant findings are communicated throughout the company to help prevent recurrence
The TDI process at the plant has hazards that are carefully managed to ensure continued safe operation. The prevention program o

utlined above is applied to the TDI process. Collectively, these prevention program activities help prevent potential accidental releases that could be caused by equipment failures, human errors, and by management system failures.
In addition to the accidental release prevention program, the facility has safety features on many units to help contain or control a release and mitigate the consequences a release. The following types of safety features are used in various parts of the TDI process:
	Release Prevention 
o	TDI tanks are interconnected with overflow piping to prevent releases due to overfill 
o	Seal-less magnetic drive TDI centrifugal pumps to prevent release from pumps
o	Redundant level sensors at 90% and 95% capacity with automatic shut off and alarm functions
o	Pressure/vacuum relief devices on vessels to prevent rupture or collapse
o	TDI railcar is surrounded by an outer shell filled with insulation
o	TDI railcars are top unloaded, meaning offloading processes are conducted through a nozzle in the top of the tank
	Release Containment
o	Concrete curbing to contain TDI liquid releases
o	TDI tanks are located inside an enclosed building, which further prevents release to the community
o	Rail cars are contained in an indoor rail pit with concrete curbing to contain chemical releases
	Release Mitigation
o	Fire suppression and extinguishing systems
o	Remote shutdown of unloading and transfer pumps
o	Trained emergency response personnel
o	Personal protective equipment (e.g., protective clothing, self-contained breathing apparatus, etc.)
o	Spill containment equipment

4.	Five-Year Accident History
Future Foam has had no releases of TDI in the last 5 years that resulted in deaths, injuries, or significant property damage on site, or known deaths, injuries, evacuations, sheltering-in-place, property damage, or environmental damage off site. Future Foam has also had no reportable quantity (RQ) releases over the past 5 years. 

5.	Emergency Response Program
Our

emergency response program is based on the requirements in OSHAs emergency action and fire prevention plan regulation, OSHAs hazardous waste and emergency operations regulation, and EPAs emergency response program requirements in its RMP rule. Our program consists of procedures for responding to a release of TDI. The procedures address all aspects of emergency response, including proper first aid and medical treatment for exposures, evacuation plans and accounting for personnel after an evacuation, notification of local emergency response agencies and the public via the Regional Emergency Planning Committee (REPC) if a release occurs, and post-incident cleanup and decontamination requirements. In addition, the plant has procedures that address inspection of emergency response equipment. Employees receive training in these procedures as necessary to perform their specific emergency response duties. The emergency response program is updated when necessary, based on modifications made to plant processes or other facilities. Personnel affected by changes in the program are informed and or trained on those changes.
The overall emergency response program for the plant is coordinated with the REPC through the Mansfield Fire Department. This coordination includes sharing information via the Tier II report system and involving the fire department in on-site drills. The plant has around-the-clock communications capability with the appropriate REPC officials and emergency response organizations such as the fire department. This provides a means of notifying the public of an incident, if necessary, as well as facilitating quick response to an incident. 

6.	Planned Changes to Improve Safety
We strive to continuously improve the safety of our plant TDI process through periodic safety reviews and a program of soliciting safety suggestions from employees. Our hazard review and incident investigation programs are especially designed to identify needed process safety improvements
, some of which result in changes to the processes.
